title: One tiny rule, z² + c, draws a shape with new detail at every zoom, forever

cover.alt: The Mandelbrot set: a black shape like a heart with a round bulb attached, fringed with tiny buds, on a blue background.

body: Pick a number c (complex numbers allowed), start at zero and repeat one step: square it, then add c. For some values of c the results stay small forever; for others they race off to infinity. The **Mandelbrot set** is every c that stays bounded, and colouring the rest by how fast they escape gives this picture. Its edge is infinitely complicated: zooming in reveals ever finer spirals, and slightly distorted copies of the whole set at every scale. Robert Brooks and Peter Matelski first drew it in 1978; Benoit Mandelbrot made his images at IBM in 1980.

slides.alt: A continuous zoom into the Mandelbrot set. Starting from the whole black shape, the view dives into the crack between two bulbs, past glowing spirals, until a tiny black copy of the whole set appears and the dive continues into its edge.
slides.caption: The dive starts from the whole Mandelbrot set and heads into one crack in its edge. Spirals give way to a tiny copy of the whole set, and the same crack appears again.
slides.credit: SimsContPics, WebM by Nick Birse · Public domain · excerpt

slides.heading: Repeat forever: does the number stay small?
Start at 0, square, add c, repeat. In or out?
slides.explanation: A value is in the set if the numbers stay bounded. Once they get more than 2 away from zero they are certain to run off to infinity.

slides.label: the fractal dimension of the set’s edge
slides.text: A smooth curve has dimension 1 and a filled area 2. The edge is so wrinkled that it scores as high as an area, as Mitsuhiro Shishikura proved.

slides.prompt: Zooms seem to show little islands floating off the main shape. Is the Mandelbrot set one piece, or many?
slides.detail: Adrien Douady and John Hubbard proved it is connected, although Mandelbrot had first guessed it was not. They also named it after him.
